docs.title: About Me
docs.text: My academic path so far has been intentionally broad: rather than committing early to a single narrow specialization, I chose to build working knowledge across hydrology, water quality modeling, machine learning, and civil engineering practice. This breadth has made me adaptable. Across every project I have taken on, I invested the time needed to learn whatever tools or methods the problem demanded, from ensemble ML models to process-based water quality simulators. I now see doctoral study as the natural next step: an opportunity to convert this broad foundation into deep, sustained expertise in a focused research direction, and to make meaningful scientific contributions that bridge data-driven modeling with environmental and water resources engineering.

docs.title: Research Vision
docs.text:
Through my thesis work, in which I engaged with both physically-based and data-driven hydrological models, I came to realize that combining these two approaches holds significant untapped potential. Physically-based models capture the underlying processes governing hydrological and water quality systems, but are often limited by simplifying assumptions and high computational cost. Data-driven methods, in contrast, can capture complex, nonlinear patterns directly from data, yet often lack physical interpretability. I am convinced that the next generation of environmental modeling lies at the intersection of these two paradigms, particularly through hybrid and physics-informed machine learning approaches.

The growing availability of computational power, advances in deep learning algorithms, and the increasing richness of satellite and ground-based observational data have created unprecedented opportunities to address the long-standing limitations of purely physics-based models. My research vision is to develop hybrid modeling frameworks that combine the mechanistic rigor of process-based simulators with the flexibility and predictive power of modern machine learning, applied to challenges in hydrology and water quality. I am particularly interested in how such frameworks can improve prediction accuracy in data-scarce regions, enhance the interpretability of AI-based models, and remain robust under changing environmental and climatic conditions.

Ultimately, I believe research achieves its full value when it moves beyond methodological novelty and translates into tools that support real-world decision-making and environmental policy. This sense of purpose, connecting rigorous science with practical impact, is what continues to drive my pursuit of doctoral research.

docs.title: Research Interests
docs.text:
• Water and Environmental Modeling

    Developing and applying physically-based and conceptual hydrological models to better understand and simulate water and environmental systems under changing climatic and human pressures.

  • Uncertainty and Sensitivity Analysis

    Investigating classical and novel sensitivity analysis methods to identify key parameters and sources of uncertainty in hydrological models, with the goal of improving model reliability and interpretability.

  • Machine Learning and Deep Learning

    Exploring how machine learning and deep learning techniques can complement physically-based models — leveraging satellite and ground-based data to address their limitations and enhance predictive performance.

docs.title: Evaluating Machine Learning Methods for Variance-based Sensitivity Analysis in Hydrological Models
docs.text:
Global sensitivity analysis (GSA) is essential for understanding which parameters govern hydrological model behavior, but classical variance-based estimators (e.g., Sobol indices) become computationally expensive at scale. This thesis benchmarked a machine-learning surrogate — Random Forest Permutation Variable Importance (RF-PVI) — against the Sobol total-order index across convergence, robustness, accuracy, and computational cost, using the HBV hydrological model on the Bow River Basin as a case study.

Graphical abstract — Monte Carlo sampling, HBV model runs, RF-PVI computation, and Sobol total-order estimation, evaluated against convergence, robustness, accuracy, and computational time. HBVSobol IndicesRandom ForestMonte CarloPython
